title: Season of Migration to the North
source:
{{Short description|1966 novel by Tayeb Salih}} {{Infobox book | | name = Season of Migration to the North | original_title = موسم الهجرة إلى الشمال
''{{Transliteration|ar|DIN|Mawsim al-Hiǧra ilā ash-Shamāl}}''. | translator = [[Denys Johnson-Davies]] | image = Season of migration to the north.jpg | alt = Season of Migration to the North | caption = Front cover of Heinemann edition of the novel | author = [[Tayeb Salih]] | cover_artist = | publication_place = [[Sudan]] | language = [[Arabic language|Arabic]] | series = | genre = | publication_date = 1966 | media_type = Print ([[Hardcover]] and [[Paperback]]) | pages = 169 pp (Heinemann edition) | isbn = 0-435-90630-5 | preceded_by = | followed_by = }} '''''Season of Migration to the North''''' ({{langx|ar|موسم الهجرة إلى الشمال}} {{Transliteration|ar|DIN|Mawsim al-Hijrah ilâ al-Shamâl}}) is a novel by the Sudanese writer [[Tayeb Salih]], first published serially in the [[Beirut]] journal ''[[Hiwar (magazine)|Hiwâr]]'' in 1966. It became Salih's best known work and is considered a classic of [[postcolonial literature]]. The main concern of the novel is the impact of [[British colonialism]] and European modernity on rural African societies in general and Sudanese culture and identity in particular.Waïl S. Hassan, Tayeb Salih: Ideology and the Craft of Fiction, Syracuse University Press, 2003. The novel reflects the conflicts of modern [[Sudan]] and depicts the brutal history of [[European colonialism]] as shaping the reality of contemporary Sudanese society. Damascus-based Arab Literary Academy named it one of the best novels in [[Arabic]] of the 20th century. ''Mawsim al-Hijrah ilâ al-Shamâl'' is considered to be an important turning point in the development of postcolonial narratives that focus on the encounter between East and West. The novel has been translated into over twenty languages.Johnson-Davies, ''Memories In Translation: A Life Between The Lines Of Arabic Literature'', p 85 Salih was fluent in both English and Arabic, but chose to pen this novel in Arabic.{{Cite web|url=http://www.gradesaver.com/season-of-migration-to-the-north|title=Season of Migration to the North Study Guide|last=GradeSaver|website=www.gradesaver.com|access-date=2016-04-08}} The English translation by [[Denys Johnson-Davies]] was published in 1969 as part of the influential [[Heinemann African Writers Series]]. The novel is a counternarrative to ''[[Heart of Darkness]]''. It was described by [[Edward Said]] as one of the six great novels in Arabic literature.{{Cite news |last=Mahjoub |first=Jamal |date=2009-02-20 |title=Tayeb Salih |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2009/feb/20/obituary-tayeb-salih |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251003003152/https://www.theguardian.com/books/2009/feb/20/obituary-tayeb-salih |archive-date=3 October 2025 |access-date=2025-09-19 |newspaper=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} In 2001, it was selected by a panel of Arab writers and critics as the most important Arab novel of the 20th century.{{Cite web|url=https://www.rifflebooks.com/books/58768|title=Season of Migration to the North (New York Review Books Classics)|website=Rifflebooks.com|access-date=2016-04-08}} == Plot == ''Mawsim al-Hijrah ilâ al-Shamâl'' is the story of the “traveled man,” the African who has returned from schooling abroad, told to an unspecified audience by an unnamed narrator. The narrator returns to his Sudanese village of [[Wad Hamid]] on the [[Nile]] in the 1950s after writing a [[Thesis|doctoral thesis]] on ‘the life of an obscure English poet.' Mustafa Sa'eed, the main protagonist of the novel, is a child of [[British colonialism]], and a fruit of colonial education. He is also a monstrous product of his time. [[File:Westminster Bridge, Building og Parliament, Big Ben, London - no-nb digifoto 20150218 00197 NB MIT FNR 19210.jpg|thumb|London in the 1920s, where Mustafa Saeed studied]] The unnamed narrator is eager to make a contribution to the new postcolonial life of his country. On his arrival home, the narrator encounters a new villager named Mustafa Sa'eed who exhibits none of the adulation for his achievements that most others do, and he displays an antagonistically aloof nature. Mustafa betrays his past one drunken evening by wistfully reciting poetry in fluent English, leaving the narrator resolute to discover the stranger's identity. The narrator later asks Mustafa about his past, and Mustafa tells him much of his story, often saying "I am no [[Othello (character)|Othello]], Othello was a lie," as well as "I am a lie." The narrator becomes fascinated by Mustafa, and learns that Mustafa was also a precocious student educated in the West but that he held a violent, hateful and complex relationship with his western identity and acquaintances.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} The story of Mustafa's troubled past in Europe, and in particular his love affairs with British women, form the center of the novel. Mustafa attracts the women by appealing to their [[Orientalism|Orientalist]] fantasies, and all of these relationships end in tragedy. Three of the women commit suicide and the fourth, Mustafa's wife, is murdered by him. He stands trial for the murder and serves time in an English jail. In the dramatic present, Mustafa drowns in the [[Nile]], and his widow, Hosna, is pressured to remarry. She refuses, because she does not want to marry after her husband. She tries to appeal to the narrator, who was appointed the guardian of her sons in Mustafa's will. The narrator does try to foil the marriage, before it can take place, but he spends most of his time in Khartoum and therefore cannot exert much influence on the village. Hosna is married to Wad Rayyes against her will, and when he attempts to forcefully consummate the marriage, she kills him first and then proceeds to kill herself. Both are then buried without a funeral. The stories of Mustafa's past life in England and the repercussions on the village around him, take their toll on the narrator, who is driven to the edge of sanity. In the final chapter, the narrator is floating in the Nile, precariously between life and death, and resolves to rid himself of Mustafa's lingering presence, and to stand as an influential individual in his own right. In the middle of the Nile, he yells, "Help! Help!". His desire to live is nothing but a clinging to hope despite all the struggles and crises he has endured. The novel ends upon that cry, and it is unclear whether his decision is too late, whether it is the right one, and whether he, others, and the country itself will receive the help needed.{{Cite web|url=http://www.wordswithoutborders.org/book-review/season-of-migration-to-the-north|title=Season of Migration to the North – Words Without Borders|last=Harss|first=Marina|website=Words Without Borders|access-date=2016-04-08}} == Background == In January 1899, a [[Condominium (international law)|condominium]], or joint-authority, was established to rule over Sudan by Britain and Egypt.{{Cite web |title=Sudan – THE ANGLO-EGYPTIAN CONDOMINIUM, 1899–1955 |url=http://countrystudies.us/sudan/15.htm |access-date=2016-04-08 |website=countrystudies.us}} Sudan gained independence in 1956, but was then engulfed in two prolonged civil wars for much of the remainder of the 20th century.{{Cite web |title=The World Factbook |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/sudan/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111020040/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/sudan |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 11, 2021 |access-date=2016-04-08 |website=www.cia.gov}} This novel is set in the 1960s, a significant and tumultuous time in [[History of Sudan#Independent Sudan (1956 to present)|Sudan's history]]. Tayeb Salih wrote his novel ''Season of Migration to the North'' in the mid-1960s. Some sources indicate that he began writing it during a vacation in southern France in 1962, then stopped for four years before later completing it.{{Cite web |title=كاتب بريطاني: "موسم الهجرة للشمال" أهم رواية عربية |trans-title=British writer: "Season of Migration to the North" is the most important Arabic novel |url=https://www.aljazeera.net/culture/2017/10/5/%d9%83%d8%a7%d8%aa%d8%a8-%d8%a8%d8%b1%d9%8a%d8%b7%d8%a7%d9%86%d9%8a-%d9%85%d9%88%d8%b3%d9%85-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%87%d8%ac%d8%b1%d8%a9-%d9%84%d9%84%d8%b4%d9%85%d8%a7%d9%84-%d8%a3%d9%87%d9%85 |access-date=2025-09-12 |website=الجزيرة.نت |language=ar}} This was in contrast to his successful novel ''[[The Wedding of Zein]]'', which he wrote in three months in the late 1950s.{{Cite web |author=محمد رضا نصر الله |date=2017-04-28 |title=مقابلة الطيب صالح مع محمد رضا نصرالله في برنامج (هذا هو) عام 1993 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yx9yvKsSA-A |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230511200839/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yx9yvKsSA-A |archive-date=2023-05-11 |website=YouTube |access-date=2025-10-10 |url-status=live }} The novel was first published in serialized form in the magazine ''[[Hiwar (magazine)|Hiwar]]'', which was issued in Beirut (and later moved to Doha). Critic [[Raja'a Al-Naqqash]] invited the author to publish it as a serial in the magazine in 1966.{{Cite web |author=العدم |first=حسن |title=موسم الهجرة إلى الشمال.. عبقرية الطيب صالح التي لا تشيخ |trans-title=Season of Migration to the North: Tayeb Salih's ageless genius |url=https://doc.aljazeera.net/portrait/2020/9/22/%d9%85%d9%88%d8%b3%d9%85-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%87%d8%ac%d8%b1%d8%a9-%d8%a5%d9%84%d9%89-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b4%d9%85%d8%a7%d9%84-%d8%b9%d8%a8%d9%82%d8%b1%d9%8a%d8%a9-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b7%d9%8a%d8%a8-%d8%b5%d8%a7 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250723033748/https://doc.aljazeera.net/portrait/2020/9/22/%D9%85%D9%88%D8%B3%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D8%AC%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%B9%D8%A8%D9%82%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B7%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%B5%D8%A7 |archive-date=2025-07-23 |access-date=2025-09-12 |website=الجزيرة الوثائقية |language=ar |url-status=live }} The novel appeared in issues 5 and 6 of ''Hiwar'' (September 1966),{{Cite web |date=2020-04-16 |title=100 رواية أفريقية.. "موسم الهجرة إلى الشمال" أيقونة الطيب صالح عن الغرب |trans-title=100 African Novels: "Season of Migration to the North" by Tayeb Salih, an icon of the West |url=https://www.youm7.com/story/2020/4/16/100-%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A3%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%82%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D9%85%D9%88%D8%B3%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D8%AC%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%A3%D9%8A%D9%82%D9%88%D9%86%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B7%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%B5%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AD/4726650 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230929002625/https://www.youm7.com/story/2020/4/16/100-%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A3%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%82%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D9%85%D9%88%D8%B3%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D8%AC%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%A3%D9%8A%D9%82%D9%88%D9%86%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B7%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%B5%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AD/4726650 |archive-date=2023-09-29 |access-date=2025-09-12 |website=اليوم السابع |language=ar |url-status=live }} then was collected into a book and released by Dar al-Awda in Beirut that same year. Later, Dar al-Hilal in Cairo republished it in the ''Hilal Novels'' series. The novel attracted the attention of readers and critics from its first release, and was soon translated into English in 1969 by the translator [[Denys Johnson-Davies]].{{Cite web|title=ذكريات مع الطيب صالح. بقلم Denys Johnson-Davies مترجم رواية موسم الهجرة إلى الشمال|url=https://alantologia.com/blogs/59239/|access-date=2025-09-19|website=الأنطولوجيا|date=2022-07-16|language=ar-AR}} The English translation was celebrated in London, and was praised by British newspapers at the time, with ''[[The Sunday Times]]'' naming it the novel of the year.{{Cite web|date=2014-07-22|title=Tayeb Salih's 'Season of Migration to the North': Acclaimed for the Wrong Reason|url=https://arablit.org/2014/07/22/tayeb-salihs-season-of-migration-to-the-north-acclaimed-for-the-wrong-reason/|access-date=2025-10-10|website=ARABLIT & ARABLIT QUARTERLY|language=en-US}} This was followed by translations into many languages (it is said to have exceeded 21 languages), which contributed to the worldwide spread of the novel's reputation.{{Cite web |author=Lalami |first=Lailan |title=SEASON OF MIGRATION TO THE NORTH by Tayeb Salih: Introduction by Laila Lalami |url=https://images.penguinrandomhouse.com/promo_image/9781590173022_7138.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240428102525/https://images.penguinrandomhouse.com/promo_image/9781590173022_7138.pdf |archive-date=2024-04-28 |access-date=2025-09-19 |website=Penguin/NYRB |url-status=live }} In ''[[The Guardian]]'''s obituary for Tayeb Salih in 2009, the paper noted that "the novel was translated into more than thirty languages". == Relation to other texts == It has been compared in many ways to [[Joseph Conrad]]'s ''[[Heart of Darkness]]''. Both novels explore [[cultural hybridity]], cross-colonial experiences, and [[Orientalism]]. The novel is also set in the same village, Wad Hamid, as some of Salih's other works, including ''[[The Wedding of Zein]], Bandarshah'', and others. Many of the novel's characters, such as Mahjoub and the narrator, recur in these other works as well. Thus, Ami Elad-Boulaski writes that Salih's depiction of Wad Hamid is more fully realized because a reader can track the development of characters throughout multiple novels and short stories.{{Cite journal|last=Elad-Bouskila|first=Ami|year=1998|title=Shaping the Cast of Characters: The Case of Al-Tayyib Salih|journal=Journal of Arabic Literature|volume=29| issue=2 |pages=59–84}} == Controversy == ''Season of Migration to the North'' was initially published in 1966, in serialized form, by ''Hiwar'', a Beirut-based [[literary magazine]] that was covertly established and funded by the [[Central Intelligence Agency|CIA]].{{cite journal |last1=Holt |first1=Elizabeth M. |title=Al-Tayyib Salih's Season of Migration to the North, the CIA, and the Cultural Cold War after Bandung |journal=Research in African Literatures |date=Fall 2019 |volume=50 |issue=3 |doi=10.2979/reseafrilite.50.3.07 }} The novel was banned in the author's native [[Sudan]] for a period of time starting in 1983 because its graphic sexual imagery offended the Islamic government. Today the novel is readily available in Sudan. == Theater == * ''Season of Migration to the North'', adapted and directed by [[Ouriel Zohar]], starring [[Mohammad Bakri]]. Bakri won the award for best actor in the 1993 [[Acco Festival of Alternative Israeli Theatre]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2022}} == Editions in print == *{{ISBN|0-435-90630-5}} ''Season of Migration to the North'', 1969 Heinemann *{{ISBN|0-935576-29-0}} ''Season of Migration to the North'' (hardcover), 1989 M.
